problems.title: Top three products per category
problems.statement_md: A grocery-delivery app wants the best sellers in each category. Total the `line_total` of every product, then return the products whose total revenue is among the **three highest distinct revenue values** in their category: if two products tie, they share a place, and every product tied at the cutoff is kept. Return `category`, `product`, `total_revenue`, ordered by `category`, then `total_revenue` descending, then `product`.

tables.name: basket_lines
tables.description_md: One row per product line in a delivered basket.

hints_md: Aggregate to one row per product first, then rank those totals.
Decide how ties should consume rank positions before choosing the ranking function.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: top N per group with ties kept.

Approach in words: build per-product totals in a CTE or subquery, rank them inside each category, filter on the rank in an outer query (window results cannot be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE).

Syntax reminder: `fn() OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY metric DESC)`.

Trap: the three ranking functions treat ties differently. Ask yourself whether a gap in rank numbers after a tie should shrink the cutoff.

solutions.label: DENSE_RANK on aggregated totals
solutions.explain_md: Dense ranks do not skip numbers after ties, so rank <= 3 keeps every product tied at the cutoff.
solutions.sql:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT category, product, SUM(line_total) AS total_revenue
  FROM basket_lines
  GROUP BY category, product
), ranked AS (
  SELECT category, product, total_revenue,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM totals
)
SELECT category, product, total_revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY category, total_revenue DESC, product;

solutions.label: Count distinct higher totals
solutions.explain_md: A product qualifies if fewer than three distinct totals in its category are larger than its own.
solutions.sql:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT category, product, SUM(line_total) AS total_revenue
  FROM basket_lines
  GROUP BY category, product
)
SELECT t.category, t.product, t.total_revenue
FROM totals t
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x.total_revenue)
       FROM totals x
       WHERE x.category = t.category AND x.total_revenue > t.total_revenue) < 3
ORDER BY t.category, t.total_revenue DESC, t.product;

traps.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER always returns exactly three rows per category and breaks ties arbitrarily, so tied products at the cutoff are dropped.
traps.sql:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT category, product, SUM(line_total) AS total_revenue
  FROM basket_lines
  GROUP BY category, product
), ranked AS (
  SELECT category, product, total_revenue,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, product) AS rn
  FROM totals
)
SELECT category, product, total_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, total_revenue DESC, product;

problems.title: Lowest-rated shops per region
problems.statement_md: Operations wants to coach the weakest partner shops. Shops with no rating yet (`avg_rating` is NULL) are not rated and must be ignored. For each region, return the shops whose rating is one of the **two lowest distinct rating values** in that region (ties share a place and are all kept). Return `region`, `shop_name`, `avg_rating`, ordered by `region`, `avg_rating`, `shop_name`.

tables.name: shops
tables.description_md: One row per partner shop. `avg_rating` is NULL until a shop has reviews.

hints_md: Where do NULLs land when you sort ascending in MySQL?
Remove the unrated shops before ranking, not after.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: bottom N per group with ties and NULLs.

Approach in words: filter out NULL ratings, rank ascending within region with a ranking function that does not skip numbers after ties, keep the first two places.

Syntax reminder: `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY metric ASC)`.

Trap: in MySQL, NULL sorts first in an ascending ORDER BY, so unrated rows can look like the worst performers. A WHERE after the window does not help, because the NULL row has already taken a rank.

solutions.label: Filter NULLs, then DENSE_RANK ascending
solutions.explain_md: Filtering inside the CTE keeps NULL rows from taking rank 1; dense ranks keep ties at the cutoff.
solutions.sql:
WITH rated AS (
  SELECT region, shop_name, avg_rating,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY avg_rating ASC) AS rnk
  FROM shops
  WHERE avg_rating IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT region, shop_name, avg_rating
FROM rated
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY region, avg_rating, shop_name;

solutions.label: Count distinct lower ratings
solutions.explain_md: A shop is kept if fewer than two distinct ratings in its region are lower than its own.
solutions.sql:
SELECT s.region, s.shop_name, s.avg_rating
FROM shops s
WHERE s.avg_rating IS NOT NULL
  AND (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x.avg_rating)
       FROM shops x
       WHERE x.region = s.region AND x.avg_rating < s.avg_rating) < 2
ORDER BY s.region, s.avg_rating, s.shop_name;

traps.explain_md: Ranking before removing NULLs lets the unrated shop take rank 1 (NULL sorts first ascending), pushing real low performers out.
traps.sql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT region, shop_name, avg_rating,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY avg_rating ASC) AS rnk
  FROM shops
)
SELECT region, shop_name, avg_rating FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 2 AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY region, avg_rating, shop_name;

problems.title: Latest plan change per user
problems.statement_md: A subscription app logs every plan change in `profile_changes`. Return each user's current plan: the row with the latest `updated_at`. When two changes for a user carry the exact same timestamp, the one with the **higher `change_id`** is considered later. Return `user_id`, `plan`, `updated_at`, ordered by `user_id`.

tables.name: profile_changes
tables.description_md: One row per plan change. `change_id` is not guaranteed to follow time order.

hints_md: Number each user's rows from newest to oldest; what must the ORDER BY contain to be deterministic?
Keep only the first row of each numbering.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: latest record per key (deduplication).

Approach in words: number rows per key newest-first with an ORDER BY that includes a tie-breaker, then keep number 1.

Syntax reminder: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC)`.

Traps: joining back to `MAX(ts)` returns both rows of a timestamp tie; `MAX(id)` is only the latest row when ids follow time.

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER with tie-breaker
solutions.explain_md: The secondary sort on change_id makes the ordering total, so exactly one row gets number 1.
solutions.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT user_id, plan, updated_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, change_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM profile_changes
)
SELECT user_id, plan, updated_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY user_id;

solutions.label: Correlated LIMIT 1
solutions.explain_md: For each row, check whether it is the first row of that user's newest-first ordering.
solutions.sql:
SELECT p.user_id, p.plan, p.updated_at
FROM profile_changes p
WHERE p.change_id = (SELECT q.change_id
                     FROM profile_changes q
                     WHERE q.user_id = p.user_id
                     ORDER BY q.updated_at DESC, q.change_id DESC
                     LIMIT 1)
ORDER BY p.user_id;

traps.explain_md: Joining to MAX(updated_at) keeps both rows when two changes share the latest timestamp.
traps.sql:
SELECT p.user_id, p.plan, p.updated_at
FROM profile_changes p
JOIN (SELECT user_id, MAX(updated_at) AS mx FROM profile_changes GROUP BY user_id) m
  ON m.user_id = p.user_id AND m.mx = p.updated_at
ORDER BY p.user_id;

traps.explain_md: Taking the highest change_id assumes ids follow time order, which they do not for every user.
traps.sql:
SELECT p.user_id, p.plan, p.updated_at
FROM profile_changes p
WHERE p.change_id = (SELECT MAX(q.change_id) FROM profile_changes q WHERE q.user_id = p.user_id)
ORDER BY p.user_id;

problems.title: Third payment per user
problems.statement_md: Marketing wants to reward the moment a customer makes their **third payment**. Return that payment for every user who has at least three: `user_id`, `payment_id`, `paid_at`, `amount`. Payments are ordered by `paid_at`; when two payments share the exact timestamp the lower `payment_id` comes first. Order the output by `user_id`.

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: One row per payment. `payment_id` does not always follow time order.

hints_md: You need a position number that never repeats, even for equal timestamps.
Filter on the position in an outer query.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: the Nth row per group (exactly one row per position).

Approach in words: number each user's payments chronologically with a full tie-breaker, keep number 3.

Syntax reminder: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY ts, id)`.

Trap: RANK and DENSE_RANK let ties share a number, so a tie at position 2 can leave nobody at 3 (RANK) or move the third row (DENSE_RANK).

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER gives each payment a unique position within the user.
solutions.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, payment_id, paid_at, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id) AS rn
  FROM payments
)
SELECT user_id, payment_id, paid_at, amount
FROM numbered
WHERE rn = 3
ORDER BY user_id;

solutions.label: Count earlier payments
solutions.explain_md: A payment is the third when exactly two payments come before it in (paid_at, payment_id) order.
solutions.sql:
SELECT p.user_id, p.payment_id, p.paid_at, p.amount
FROM payments p
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)
       FROM payments q
       WHERE q.user_id = p.user_id
         AND (q.paid_at < p.paid_at OR (q.paid_at = p.paid_at AND q.payment_id < p.payment_id))) = 2
ORDER BY p.user_id;

traps.explain_md: RANK lets the two payments at the same timestamp share position 2, so position 3 does not exist for that user.
Ordering by payment_id instead of time picks the wrong row when ids are out of order.

problems.title: Running balance per account
problems.statement_md: A payments platform keeps a ledger of credits (positive) and debits (negative). For every entry return the account's running balance **after that entry**, entries ordered by `entry_date` then `entry_id`, restarting at each account. Return `entry_id`, `account_id`, `entry_date`, `amount`, `running_balance`, ordered by `account_id`, `entry_date`, `entry_id`.

tables.name: ledger_entries
tables.description_md: One row per ledger entry; several entries can fall on the same day.

hints_md: The frame decides whether same-day rows see each other. Which frame do you get if you write none?
Make the ORDER BY unique so the order inside a day is defined.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: running total per partition.

Approach in words: SUM over a window partitioned by account, ordered by date and id, with the frame stated explicitly so each row sums only rows up to itself.

Syntax reminder: `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY d, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

Trap: with ORDER BY but no frame the default is RANGE, which treats rows with equal sort keys as peers and gives them all the same total.

solutions.label: SUM OVER with ROWS frame
solutions.explain_md: An explicit ROWS frame counts physical rows, so each entry gets its own running value.
solutions.sql:
SELECT entry_id, account_id, entry_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY entry_date, entry_id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_balance
FROM ledger_entries
ORDER BY account_id, entry_date, entry_id;

solutions.label: Self-join
solutions.explain_md: Sum every entry of the same account that sorts at or before the current one.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.entry_id, e.account_id, e.entry_date, e.amount,
       SUM(x.amount) AS running_balance
FROM ledger_entries e
JOIN ledger_entries x
  ON x.account_id = e.account_id
 AND (x.entry_date < e.entry_date OR (x.entry_date = e.entry_date AND x.entry_id <= e.entry_id))
GROUP BY e.entry_id, e.account_id, e.entry_date, e.amount
ORDER BY e.account_id, e.entry_date, e.entry_id;

traps.explain_md: Ordering by date only uses the default RANGE frame, so same-day entries all show the end-of-day balance.
traps.sql:
SELECT entry_id, account_id, entry_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY entry_date) AS running_balance
FROM ledger_entries
ORDER BY account_id, entry_date, entry_id;

problems.title: Three-day rolling average with missing days
problems.statement_md: Growth wants the average daily signups over the **last three calendar days** (the row's date and the two days before it). A calendar day with no row in `daily_signups` had zero signups, and counts as 0 inside the average, so the divisor is always 3. Return `signup_date`, `signups`, `rolling_avg_3d` (rounded to 2 decimals) for each existing row, ordered by `signup_date`.

tables.name: daily_signups
tables.description_md: One row per day that had at least one signup; quiet days are absent.

hints_md: Three rows and three days are only the same thing when no day is missing.
Either let the window frame measure days, or join each row to the dates in its range.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: rolling window over calendar time.

Approach in words: sum the signups whose date lies in [date - 2 days, date], then divide by 3.

Syntax reminders: a ROWS frame counts rows; a RANGE frame with an interval counts calendar distance: `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 2 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (ORDER BY must be a single date column). A self-join on `BETWEEN` also works.

Trap: `AVG(...) ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING` averages rows, not days.

solutions.label: Self-join on a date range
solutions.explain_md: Join each day to the days in its three-day span, sum, divide by 3.
solutions.sql:
SELECT d.signup_date, d.signups,
       ROUND(SUM(x.signups) / 3, 2) AS rolling_avg_3d
FROM daily_signups d
JOIN daily_signups x
  ON x.signup_date BETWEEN DATE_SUB(d.signup_date, INTERVAL 2 DAY) AND d.signup_date
GROUP BY d.signup_date, d.signups
ORDER BY d.signup_date;

solutions.label: RANGE frame with INTERVAL
solutions.explain_md: A RANGE frame over a date counts by calendar distance, so missing days naturally contribute nothing.
solutions.sql:
SELECT signup_date, signups,
       ROUND(SUM(signups) OVER (ORDER BY signup_date
                                RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 2 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) / 3, 2) AS rolling_avg_3d
FROM daily_signups
ORDER BY signup_date;

traps.explain_md: A ROWS frame averages the previous two existing rows, which can be many days old, and divides by the row count.
traps.sql:
SELECT signup_date, signups,
       ROUND(AVG(signups) OVER (ORDER BY signup_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_avg_3d
FROM daily_signups
ORDER BY signup_date;

problems.title: Seven-day rolling revenue with a date spine
problems.statement_md: A retail dashboard needs one row for **every calendar day** between the first and the last sale in `store_sales`, including days with no sales. For each day return `sale_date`, `daily_revenue` (0 if no sales), and `rolling_7d_revenue`, the revenue of that day and the six calendar days before it. Order by `sale_date`.

tables.name: store_sales
tables.description_md: One row per sale; days without sales have no rows at all.

hints_md: MySQL has no generate_series. A recursive CTE can walk one day at a time.
After the spine is joined to the daily totals, every row is one day, so a row-count frame becomes a day-count frame.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: date spine + rolling window.

Approach in words: find min and max date, generate every date with a recursive CTE, LEFT JOIN the aggregated daily totals, COALESCE missing days to 0, then apply the rolling frame.

Syntax reminders: `WITH RECURSIVE s AS (SELECT start_d AS d UNION ALL SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM s WHERE d < end_d)`; `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

Trap: a 7-row frame over only the days that have sales spans more than 7 days.

solutions.label: Spine, LEFT JOIN, ROWS 6 PRECEDING
solutions.explain_md: On a gap-free spine one row equals one day, so six preceding rows are six preceding days.

solutions.label: Spine with a range subquery
solutions.explain_md: For each spine date, sum the daily totals whose date is within the past seven days.
solutions.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE bounds AS (
  SELECT MIN(sale_date) AS first_d, MAX(sale_date) AS last_d FROM store_sales
), spine AS (
  SELECT first_d AS d FROM bounds
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE_ADD(s.d, INTERVAL 1 DAY) FROM spine s, bounds b WHERE s.d < b.last_d
), daily AS (
  SELECT sale_date, SUM(amount) AS rev FROM store_sales GROUP BY sale_date
)
SELECT s.d AS sale_date,
       COALESCE((SELECT rev FROM daily WHERE sale_date = s.d), 0) AS daily_revenue,
       COALESCE((SELECT SUM(x.rev) FROM daily x
                 WHERE x.sale_date BETWEEN DATE_SUB(s.d, INTERVAL 6 DAY) AND s.d), 0) AS rolling_7d_revenue
FROM spine s
ORDER BY s.d;

traps.explain_md: Windowing over only the days that have sales skips quiet days and spans more than seven calendar days.
traps.sql:
SELECT sale_date, SUM(amount) AS daily_revenue,
       SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_7d_revenue
FROM store_sales
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;

problems.title: Month-over-month revenue growth
problems.statement_md: Finance tracks `monthly_revenue`. For each month return `month_start`, `revenue`, `prev_month_revenue` and `growth_pct`, the percentage change from the **previous calendar month**, rounded to 1 decimal. If the previous calendar month has no row, `prev_month_revenue` and `growth_pct` are NULL. If the previous month's revenue is 0, `growth_pct` is NULL (no division by zero). Order by `month_start`.

tables.name: monthly_revenue
tables.description_md: One row per month that had a closed ledger; some months are missing.

hints_md: The row before in sort order is not always the month before.
Guard the denominator so a zero cannot divide.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: period-over-period comparison.

Approach in words: fetch the previous row's month and revenue (LAG, or a self-join on month + 1), accept it only if it really is one month earlier, then compute the percentage.

Syntax reminders: `LAG(col, 1) OVER (ORDER BY d)`; `TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, a, b)`; `x / NULLIF(y, 0)`.

Trap: plain LAG compares with whatever row came before, even across a missing month.

solutions.label: Self-join on previous month
solutions.explain_md: LEFT JOIN each month to the row exactly one month earlier; NULLIF guards the zero denominator.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.month_start, c.revenue,
       p.revenue AS prev_month_revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (c.revenue - p.revenue) / NULLIF(p.revenue, 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly_revenue c
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue p
  ON p.month_start = DATE_SUB(c.month_start, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
ORDER BY c.month_start;

solutions.label: LAG with a gap check
solutions.explain_md: LAG supplies the previous row; a CASE keeps it only if its month is exactly one month earlier.
solutions.sql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT month_start, revenue,
         LAG(month_start) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS pm,
         LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS pr
  FROM monthly_revenue
), y AS (
  SELECT month_start, revenue,
         CASE WHEN TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, pm, month_start) = 1 THEN pr END AS prev_month_revenue
  FROM x
)
SELECT month_start, revenue, prev_month_revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - prev_month_revenue) / NULLIF(prev_month_revenue, 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM y
ORDER BY month_start;

traps.explain_md: Plain LAG compares April with February because March has no row.
traps.sql:
SELECT month_start, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_month_revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start), 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month_start;

problems.title: Year-over-year growth per product
problems.statement_md: For every row dated in 2026, compare `units` with the same product in the **same month one year earlier**. Return `product`, `month_start`, `units`, `units_year_ago`, `yoy_pct` (percent change, 1 decimal). `units_year_ago` is NULL if that product has no row for that month last year; `yoy_pct` is also NULL when the year-ago value is missing or 0. Order by `product`, `month_start`.

tables.name: monthly_units
tables.description_md: Units sold per product per month. Not every product has every month.

hints_md: Row offsets only equal calendar offsets when the series has no gaps.
Match on product and on the date shifted back by twelve months.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: year-over-year comparison.

Approach in words: for each month find the row of the same product exactly 12 months earlier and compare. Either join the table to itself on a shifted date, or look the value up with a correlated subquery.

Syntax reminders: `DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL 12 MONTH)`; `LAG(x, 12) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY d)` is only correct on complete monthly series.

Trap: LAG with offset 12 looks 12 rows back, not 12 months back.

solutions.label: Self-join on shifted month
solutions.explain_md: LEFT JOIN each row to the same product's row 12 months earlier; filter to 2026 rows.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.product, c.month_start, c.units,
       p.units AS units_year_ago,
       ROUND(100 * (c.units - p.units) / NULLIF(p.units, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM monthly_units c
LEFT JOIN monthly_units p
  ON p.product = c.product
 AND p.month_start = DATE_SUB(c.month_start, INTERVAL 12 MONTH)
WHERE c.month_start >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY c.product, c.month_start;

solutions.label: Correlated subquery
solutions.explain_md: Look up the year-ago units per row with a scalar subquery, then compute the percentage in an outer query.
solutions.sql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT c.product, c.month_start, c.units,
         (SELECT p.units FROM monthly_units p
          WHERE p.product = c.product
            AND p.month_start = DATE_SUB(c.month_start, INTERVAL 12 MONTH)) AS units_year_ago
  FROM monthly_units c
  WHERE c.month_start >= '2026-01-01'
)
SELECT product, month_start, units, units_year_ago,
       ROUND(100 * (units - units_year_ago) / NULLIF(units_year_ago, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM x
ORDER BY product, month_start;

traps.explain_md: LAG(units, 12) goes back twelve rows. It works for the gap-free product but is NULL or wrong for the product with missing months.
traps.sql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT product, month_start, units,
         LAG(units, 12) OVER (PARTITION BY product ORDER BY month_start) AS units_year_ago
  FROM monthly_units
)
SELECT product, month_start, units, units_year_ago,
       ROUND(100 * (units - units_year_ago) / NULLIF(units_year_ago, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM x
WHERE month_start >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY product, month_start;

problems.title: Customer spend quartiles
problems.statement_md: Split customers into four spend quartiles of as-equal-as-possible size, quartile 1 being the biggest spenders. Order customers by `total_spend` descending, breaking ties by lower `customer_id` first. Return `customer_id`, `total_spend`, `spend_quartile`, ordered by `total_spend` descending, then `customer_id`.
hints_md: There is a built-in function that cuts an ordered set into N buckets.
With 10 customers the buckets cannot all hold the same number of rows; which buckets get the extras?
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: bucketing / percentile groups.

Approach in words: order customers by spend descending with a tie-break and cut into four buckets.

Syntax reminder: `NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC, id)`; when the row count is not divisible by 4 the first buckets get one extra row.

Trap: hand-made formulas based on ROW_NUMBER and COUNT often split uneven groups in a different place than NTILE does.

solutions.label: NTILE(4)
solutions.explain_md: NTILE assigns bucket numbers in order, giving leftover rows to the earliest buckets.
solutions.sql:
SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC, customer_id) AS spend_quartile
FROM customer_spend
ORDER BY total_spend DESC, customer_id;

traps.explain_md: A ROW_NUMBER/COUNT formula spreads uneven remainders differently (3,2,3,2) than NTILE (3,3,2,2).
traps.sql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC, customer_id) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM customer_spend
)
SELECT customer_id, total_spend, FLOOR((rn - 1) * 4 / n) + 1 AS spend_quartile
FROM r
ORDER BY total_spend DESC, customer_id;

traps.explain_md: Ordering ascending flips the meaning: quartile 1 becomes the smallest spenders.
traps.sql:
SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend, customer_id) AS spend_quartile
FROM customer_spend
ORDER BY total_spend DESC, customer_id;

problems.title: Top 10 percent of earners
problems.statement_md: HR wants the highest-paid 10% of employees. An employee is in the top 10% if their **position from the top** (employees with equal salary share a position, the next position skips ahead) is at most 10% of the total headcount. Return `emp_id`, `name`, `salary`, ordered by `salary` descending, then `emp_id`.
hints_md: Compare a rank with a fraction of the total headcount. Which window gives you the headcount on every row?
Multiply instead of dividing to avoid fractions.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: percentile cut-off with ties.

Approach in words: rank salaries descending with a function where equal salaries share a position, count all rows with an unpartitioned window, keep rows whose rank is within 10% of the count.

Syntax reminders: `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC)`, `COUNT(*) OVER ()`.

Trap: NTILE(10) and ROW_NUMBER always cut at an exact row count and split ties arbitrarily.

solutions.label: RANK against headcount
solutions.explain_md: Rank gives tied salaries the same position; keeping rank * 10 <= headcount keeps all ties at the cutoff.
solutions.sql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT emp_id, name, salary,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM staff
)
SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM r
WHERE rk * 10 <= n
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id;

solutions.label: Count strictly higher salaries
solutions.explain_md: An employee's position is the number of strictly higher salaries plus one.
solutions.sql:
SELECT s.emp_id, s.name, s.salary
FROM staff s
WHERE ((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM staff x WHERE x.salary > s.salary) + 1) * 10 <= (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM staff)
ORDER BY s.salary DESC, s.emp_id;

traps.explain_md: NTILE(10) cuts exactly two rows and splits the tie at 190 arbitrarily.

problems.title: Long gaps between purchases
problems.statement_md: Retention wants to see win-back purchases. For each purchase that happened **more than 14 days** after the same user's previous purchase, return `purchase_id`, `user_id`, `purchased_on`, `days_since_prev`, and `next_item`: the item of that user's next purchase (NULL if there is none). Purchases are ordered by `purchased_on`, ties by `purchase_id`. Order the output by `user_id`, `purchased_on`, `purchase_id`.

tables.name: purchases
tables.description_md: One row per purchase. `purchase_id` does not always follow date order.

hints_md: You need both the previous and the next row of each user, so compute them before you filter.
Subtracting two dates in MySQL is done with a dedicated function.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: consecutive-event gaps (LAG and LEAD).

Approach in words: in a CTE compute the previous date and the next item per user over a fully ordered window; filter on the gap in the outer query.

Syntax reminders: `LAG(d) OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY d, id)`, `LEAD(item) OVER (...)`, `DATEDIFF(later, earlier)`.

Trap: ordering by id instead of date, and filtering rows before the LEAD is computed.

solutions.label: LAG and LEAD in a CTE
solutions.explain_md: Both neighbours come from the same fully ordered window; the gap filter happens afterwards so LEAD still sees every purchase.
solutions.sql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT purchase_id, user_id, purchased_on,
         DATEDIFF(purchased_on, LAG(purchased_on) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchased_on, purchase_id)) AS days_since_prev,
         LEAD(item) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchased_on, purchase_id) AS next_item
  FROM purchases
)
SELECT purchase_id, user_id, purchased_on, days_since_prev, next_item
FROM x
WHERE days_since_prev > 14
ORDER BY user_id, purchased_on, purchase_id;

solutions.label: Numbered self-join
solutions.explain_md: Number purchases per user, then join each to the row numbered one lower and one higher.
solutions.sql:
WITH n AS (
  SELECT purchase_id, user_id, purchased_on, item,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchased_on, purchase_id) AS rn
  FROM purchases
)
SELECT c.purchase_id, c.user_id, c.purchased_on,
       DATEDIFF(c.purchased_on, p.purchased_on) AS days_since_prev,
       nx.item AS next_item
FROM n c
JOIN n p ON p.user_id = c.user_id AND p.rn = c.rn - 1
LEFT JOIN n nx ON nx.user_id = c.user_id AND nx.rn = c.rn + 1
WHERE DATEDIFF(c.purchased_on, p.purchased_on) > 14
ORDER BY c.user_id, c.purchased_on, c.purchase_id;

traps.explain_md: Ordering the window by purchase_id compares purchases that are not neighbours in time.
traps.sql:
WITH x AS (
  SELECT purchase_id, user_id, purchased_on,
         DATEDIFF(purchased_on, LAG(purchased_on) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_id)) AS days_since_prev,
         LEAD(item) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_id) AS next_item
  FROM purchases
)
SELECT purchase_id, user_id, purchased_on, days_since_prev, next_item
FROM x WHERE days_since_prev > 14
ORDER BY user_id, purchased_on, purchase_id;

problems.title: First and last weigh-in per user
problems.statement_md: A fitness app wants each user's progress. Ignoring entries where `weight_kg` is NULL (a missed log), return one row per user with `first_weight_kg` (earliest `logged_on`), `last_weight_kg` (latest `logged_on`) and `change_kg` (last minus first). If two entries share a date, the lower `entry_id` is earlier. Order by `user_id`.

tables.name: weigh_ins
tables.description_md: One row per logged weigh-in; `weight_kg` is NULL when the user skipped the scale.

hints_md: There is a window function that returns the value from the first row of the frame, and one for the last.
Check which rows the default frame includes when you use the last-row function.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: first/last value per group.

Approach in words: filter out NULL weights, compute the first and last value over the whole partition, collapse to one row per user.

Syntax reminders: `FIRST_VALUE(x) OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY d, id)`; for the last row either extend the frame to `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` or run FIRST_VALUE with the opposite sort.

Trap: with ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the frame stops at the current row, so LAST_VALUE just returns the current row.

solutions.label: Explicit full frame
solutions.explain_md: Widening the frame to the whole partition lets LAST_VALUE see the last row; DISTINCT collapses the per-row repeats.
solutions.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER w AS first_weight_kg,
       LAST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER w AS last_weight_kg,
       LAST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER w - FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER w AS change_kg
FROM weigh_ins
WHERE weight_kg IS NOT NULL
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id
             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
ORDER BY user_id;

solutions.label: FIRST_VALUE twice with opposite sort
solutions.explain_md: FIRST_VALUE over the reverse ordering is the last value, and needs no custom frame.
solutions.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id) AS first_weight_kg,
       FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on DESC, entry_id DESC) AS last_weight_kg,
       FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on DESC, entry_id DESC)
         - FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id) AS change_kg
FROM weigh_ins
WHERE weight_kg IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY user_id;

traps.explain_md: LAST_VALUE with the default frame returns the current row's own weight, so DISTINCT yields many rows per user.
traps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id) AS first_weight_kg,
       LAST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id) AS last_weight_kg,
       LAST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id)
         - FIRST_VALUE(weight_kg) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY logged_on, entry_id) AS change_kg
FROM weigh_ins
WHERE weight_kg IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY user_id;

problems.title: Share of team cloud cost
problems.statement_md: Each team's cloud bill is split into services. For every row return `team`, `service`, `monthly_cost`, `pct_of_team` (the service's share of its **team's** total, as a percentage rounded to 1 decimal), and `vs_team_avg` (cost minus the team's average service cost, rounded to 2 decimals). A NULL cost (invoice pending) gives NULL in both new columns and is ignored in the team total and average. Order by `team`, `service`.

tables.name: cloud_costs
tables.description_md: One row per team and service. `monthly_cost` is NULL while the invoice is pending.

hints_md: Aggregate functions can be used as window functions with OVER.
The window needs a partition, otherwise you get a grand total.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: percentage of total / compare with group aggregate.

Approach in words: keep every row and attach the team's SUM and AVG with windows, then do the arithmetic.

Syntax reminders: `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY team)`, `AVG(x) OVER (PARTITION BY team)`; SUM and AVG skip NULLs.

Trap: `OVER ()` with no PARTITION BY divides by the grand total across all teams.

solutions.label: SUM and AVG OVER partition
solutions.explain_md: Window aggregates attach team-level values to each row without collapsing rows.
solutions.sql:
SELECT team, service, monthly_cost,
       ROUND(100 * monthly_cost / SUM(monthly_cost) OVER (PARTITION BY team), 1) AS pct_of_team,
       ROUND(monthly_cost - AVG(monthly_cost) OVER (PARTITION BY team), 2) AS vs_team_avg
FROM cloud_costs
ORDER BY team, service;

solutions.label: Join to a grouped subquery
solutions.explain_md: Compute team totals and averages with GROUP BY, join back on team.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.team, c.service, c.monthly_cost,
       ROUND(100 * c.monthly_cost / t.total_cost, 1) AS pct_of_team,
       ROUND(c.monthly_cost - t.avg_cost, 2) AS vs_team_avg
FROM cloud_costs c
JOIN (SELECT team, SUM(monthly_cost) AS total_cost, AVG(monthly_cost) AS avg_cost
      FROM cloud_costs GROUP BY team) t ON t.team = c.team
ORDER BY c.team, c.service;

traps.explain_md: Without PARTITION BY the shares are against the grand total of all teams.
traps.sql:
SELECT team, service, monthly_cost,
       ROUND(100 * monthly_cost / SUM(monthly_cost) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_team,
       ROUND(monthly_cost - AVG(monthly_cost) OVER (), 2) AS vs_team_avg
FROM cloud_costs
ORDER BY team, service;

problems.title: Median delivery time per city
problems.statement_md: MySQL has no median function. Return the **median** `minutes` per city (for an even count, the mean of the two middle values), ignoring deliveries whose `minutes` is NULL (not yet delivered). Return `city`, `median_minutes` (rounded to 1 decimal), ordered by `city`.

tables.name: delivery_times
tables.description_md: One row per delivery. `minutes` is NULL while the order is still out.

hints_md: Number the values in each city in sorted order, and also know how many values the city has.
Which one or two row numbers hold the middle, for odd and even counts?
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: median without PERCENTILE_CONT.

Approach in words: after dropping NULLs, give each value a position and each city a count; keep the middle position(s) and average them with GROUP BY.

Syntax reminders: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c ORDER BY v, id)`, `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY c)`. Alternative: number ascending and descending and keep rows where the two numbers differ by at most 1.

Trap: AVG is the mean, not the median; and COUNT(*) before dropping NULLs shifts the middle.

solutions.label: Position vs count
solutions.explain_md: For count n the middle positions are floor((n+1)/2) and floor(n/2)+1 (same row when n is odd); average them.
solutions.sql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT city, minutes,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY minutes, delivery_id) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY city) AS cnt
  FROM delivery_times
  WHERE minutes IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT city, ROUND(AVG(minutes), 1) AS median_minutes
FROM r
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((cnt + 1) / 2), FLOOR(cnt / 2) + 1)
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city;

solutions.label: Ascending and descending numbers
solutions.explain_md: The middle rows are those where the ascending and descending row numbers differ by at most 1.
solutions.sql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT city, minutes,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY minutes, delivery_id) AS asc_rn,
         CAST(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY minutes DESC, delivery_id DESC) AS SIGNED) AS desc_rn
  FROM delivery_times
  WHERE minutes IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT city, ROUND(AVG(minutes), 1) AS median_minutes
FROM r
WHERE asc_rn BETWEEN desc_rn - 1 AND desc_rn + 1
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city;

traps.explain_md: AVG returns the mean, which the long deliveries drag upward.
traps.sql:
SELECT city, ROUND(AVG(minutes), 1) AS median_minutes
FROM delivery_times
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city;

traps.explain_md: Taking only the lower middle row is wrong for cities with an even number of deliveries.
traps.sql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT city, minutes,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY minutes, delivery_id) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY city) AS cnt
  FROM delivery_times
  WHERE minutes IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT city, ROUND(minutes, 1) AS median_minutes
FROM r
WHERE rn = FLOOR((cnt + 1) / 2)
ORDER BY city;

problems.title: Service status changes
problems.statement_md: A monitor pings each service every few minutes and stores its `status`. Return one row for every **status change**: a ping whose status differs from the same service's previous ping (a service's first ping is not a change). Columns: `service`, `changed_at` (that ping's time), `from_status`, `to_status`, and `minutes_since_last_change`, the minutes since the same service's previous status change (NULL for a service's first change). Order by `service`, `changed_at`.
hints_md: First find the changes using the previous ping; then work with only those rows.
Looking back one change needs a second window, running over the already filtered rows.
problems.notes_md:
Pattern family: change detection with layered windows.

Approach in words: layer 1 attaches the previous status to each ping and keeps rows where it exists and differs; layer 2 runs LAG again over those change rows to get the previous change time.

Syntax reminders: `status <> LAG(status) OVER (PARTITION BY s ORDER BY t)`; `TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, earlier, later)`. Window results cannot be filtered in the same SELECT, so use a CTE per layer.

Trap: a LAG of the time in the first layer measures the gap since the previous ping, not the previous change.

solutions.label: Two CTE layers
solutions.explain_md: The first CTE flags changes; the second applies LAG on the filtered change rows only.
solutions.sql:
WITH p AS (
  SELECT service, checked_at, status,
         LAG(status) OVER (PARTITION BY service ORDER BY checked_at, ping_id) AS prev_status
  FROM service_pings
), ch AS (
  SELECT service, checked_at, prev_status, status,
         LAG(checked_at) OVER (PARTITION BY service ORDER BY checked_at) AS prev_change_at
  FROM p
  WHERE prev_status IS NOT NULL AND status <> prev_status
)
SELECT service, checked_at AS changed_at, prev_status AS from_status, status AS to_status,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, prev_change_at, checked_at) AS minutes_since_last_change
FROM ch
ORDER BY service, changed_at;

traps.explain_md: Computing LAG(checked_at) over all pings gives the minutes since the previous ping, not the previous change.
traps.sql:
WITH p AS (
  SELECT service, checked_at, status,
         LAG(status) OVER (PARTITION BY service ORDER BY checked_at, ping_id) AS prev_status,
         LAG(checked_at) OVER (PARTITION BY service ORDER BY checked_at, ping_id) AS prev_at
  FROM service_pings
)
SELECT service, checked_at AS changed_at, prev_status AS from_status, status AS to_status,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, prev_at, checked_at) AS minutes_since_last_change
FROM p
WHERE prev_status IS NOT NULL AND status <> prev_status
ORDER BY service, changed_at;
